summary.text: A protist is any eukaryotic organism that is not an animal, a land plant or a fungus.
Protists are mostly single-celled and take many forms, such as amoebae, ciliates and flagellates.
They live in all ecosystems, including extreme habitats, and as producers they are responsible for a large portion of global primary production and carbon fixation.

facts.label: Not a natural group
facts.value: A paraphyletic group, not a clade

facts.label: Share of diversity
facts.value: Most of eukaryotic diversity, and most remain undescribed

facts.label: Diseases they cause
facts.value: Malaria, toxoplasmosis, clubroot and potato blight

facts.label: Deep roots
facts.value: Eukaryotes split from archaea around 3 billion years ago

facts.label: Old names
facts.value: Once a kingdom called Protista or Protoctista

items.prompt: What single trait is shared by every protist and by no other organism?

options.label: None; the group is defined by exclusion

items.explain: Protists are defined as all eukaryotes that are not animals, land plants or fungi, so no unique trait unifies them. Some made transitions to multicellularity.

items.prompt: A biologist studies red algae, which were once lumped with plants. Under the current consensus, what are they?

options.label: Protists, since all eukaryotic algae fall under that label
Fungi, since they lack roots and stems
Animals, since they are not land plants

items.explain: The label protist excludes animals, land plants and fungi, which means all eukaryotic algae fall under it.

items.prompt: A protist has chloroplasts and also feeding structures that take in prey. How is its nutrition described?

options.label: Phototrophy alone, living only on light
Feeding alone, without using its chloroplasts
Mixotrophy, mixing light-powered and feeding modes

items.explain: Protists feed through specialized feeding structures or chloroplasts (phototrophy), often mixing both as mixotrophy.

items.prompt: Protists act as consumers and decomposers in ecosystems. What effect does that have on bacteria and fungi?

options.label: It regulates their populations and releases nutrients to other levels
It makes them multiply faster by feeding them
It has no effect, since protists only affect plants

items.explain: As consumers and decomposers, protists regulate fungal and bacterial populations and release nutrients to other trophic levels.

items.prompt: A farmer's potatoes die from blight while a traveller gets malaria. What links the two diseases?

options.label: Both are caused by pathogenic protists

items.explain: Pathogenic protists cause well-known human and animal diseases such as malaria and significant plant diseases like potato blight.

items.prompt: Protists left an extensive fossil record through the Phanerozoic. What did it mostly consist of?
items.explain: Throughout the Phanerozoic, protists left an extensive fossil record of primarily siliceous and calcareous shells.

beats.title: The Catch-All of Life
beats.hook: Biology has a group that is defined only by what it is not.

beats.prompt: Biologists look for one feature that every protist has and no other organism has. What do they find?
beats.explain: Protists are defined as all eukaryotes that are not animals, land plants or fungi, so there is no unique trait that unifies all protists yet excludes non-protists.

choices.label: All protists are single-celled
choices.feedback: Tempting, but several transitions to multicellularity have occurred among protists, such as seaweeds with differentiated tissues.

paragraphs.heading: Defined by what they are not
paragraphs.text: Protists are the eukaryotes left over once animals, land plants and fungi are set aside. Because the group is defined by exclusion, no single trait unites all protists and rules out everything else. Most are single cells, in forms such as amoebae, ciliates, thick-walled microalgae and, most often, flagellates.

paragraphs.heading: Not a natural group
paragraphs.text: Protists are not a natural group, or clade. They form a paraphyletic group that spans the whole eukaryote tree of life, and land plants, animals and fungi all evolved from within it. Several protist lineages became multicellular, producing giant slime molds, seaweeds with distinct tissues, and colonies that alternate between cell types. A less popular view limits protists to single-celled eukaryotes, but that overlooks these moves to multicellularity.

paragraphs.heading: Redrawing the family tree
paragraphs.text: Protists were once treated as their own kingdom, Protista or Protoctista, or split between the plant and animal kingdoms as algae and protozoa. Molecular phylogenetics and electron microscopy showed that some protists are closer kin to animals or plants than to other protists, and that algae and protozoa are intermixed. Today protists are spread across several large clades called supergroups. Archaeplastida holds red and green algae, from which land plants arose, while Opisthokonta holds fungi, animals and their single-celled relatives. Stramenopiles and Alveolata include diatoms, brown algae and dinoflagellates as well as major parasites.

paragraphs.heading: Clever cells
paragraphs.text: Protists show almost every biological trait found in eukaryotes, plus some of their own. They feed in many ways, through special feeding structures or through chloroplasts, and many mix the two, which is called mixotrophy. Many have unusual organelles, such as contractile vacuoles that help keep the cell's internal balance, or eyespots that sense light. Though long assumed to be asexual, protists can reproduce sexually and can have complex life cycles with several stages.

paragraphs.heading: Everywhere in nature
paragraphs.text: Protists live in every ecosystem, extreme ones included, as key parts of biogeochemical cycles and food webs. As producers they account for a large share of the world's primary production and carbon fixation. As consumers and decomposers they keep fungal and bacterial numbers in check and pass nutrients to other levels of the food web. Some live in partnership with corals or termites, while others are parasites behind malaria and toxoplasmosis, or plant diseases such as clubroot and potato blight. Free-living protists can also harm water life as harmful algal blooms.

paragraphs.heading: Mostly undiscovered, very old
paragraphs.text: Only a fairly small number of protist species have been described, yet environmental DNA studies show that protists make up most eukaryotic diversity, and most are still unnamed. Their early history matches that of eukaryotes as a whole, which branched off from archaea roughly 3 billion years ago. After the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) appeared, its descendants diversified rapidly over 300 million years into the modern supergroups. Through the Phanerozoic, protists took on the forms that dominate ecosystems today, leaving a rich fossil record of mostly siliceous and calcareous shells.
